catalog_quote: The Chilliwack dialect of Halkomelem has three degrees of phonemic pitched stress: /´/ primary or high-pitch stress, /`/ secondary or mid-pitch stress, and (unmarked) low-pitch unstressed. ... Stress occurs impartially in open (vowel-final) or closed (consonant-final) syllables. And stress can occur on any syllable (first, second, third, etc., even seventh or eighth) counting from the front or from the end. The statements made about stress in the last two sentences apply also to vowel length and vowel phonemes of all qualities. sweep_summary: Halkomelem (halk1245) is not in the catalog. The only title-sweep hit, Zimmermann 2013 (Lingua 134:1-26, doi 10.1016/j.lingua.2013.06.001), is closed access everywhere checked (OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar: no repository copy, abstract withheld; ScienceDirect 403), and her two 2009 Halkomelem handouts on uni-leipzig.de are unreachable (server hangs; no Wayback snapshot), so it stays unread: a theoretical prosodic-morphology paper on Upriver Halkomelem allomorphy whose stress facts would be second-hand from Galloway 1993 (medium priority; Galloway 1993 itself remains the high-value acquisition). First-hand stress statements already on file and read this sweep: Galloway 1977 (Upriver/Chilliwack: three phonemic pitched-stress degrees, stress on any syllable, not positionally predictable; sec. 2.2 pp. 46-47) and Bianco 1998 (Island/Cowichan roots: leftmost syllable default overridden by vowel sonority, >95% of roots; pp. 60-61). new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (realised as pitched stress: high, mid, unstressed) is phonemic and not positionally fixed: it may fall on any syllable of the word; statistically it is most often on the first or second syllable (or within the last three); in affixed words placement is governed morphologically -- unstressed/mid-stressed affixes leave the stem's stress unchanged, while inherently high-stressed prefixes, infixes and suffixes pull stress off the root (root vowel then reduces), with polysyllabic roots and inflections each tending to keep their own pattern. For Island (Cowichan) roots Bianco 1998 finds a default-leftmost pattern overridden by vowel sonority (full vowel over schwa; a > e,o > i,u), covering >95% of roots; for Musqueam, Suttles 2004 (second-hand via Wikipedia) reports primary stress usually on the first vowel, full vowel over schwa, but 'not completely predictable', with rare stress minimal pairs.
new_statements.secondary_stress: A mid-pitch 'secondary stress' /`/ is a separate phoneme (level pitch about a third above low; Sec. 1.2.20, p. 31); more than one high or mid stress can occur in a word; when a high-stressed affix takes the stress, root high stress on long vowels is sometimes retained as mid stress (Sec. 2.3.1, pp. 49-50); morphophonemic downstepping turns /´/ into /`/ after a preceding /´/ (p. 30). Suttles 2004 (via Wikipedia): secondary stress mostly in words with a stressed root plus a stressed suffix.
new_statements.exceptions: Galloway: only demonstratives and particles can occur wholly unstressed; words with more than two successive high-stressed syllables or more than four successive unstressed syllables are rare; a few words carry only mid stress in citation form (p. 31); speakers (and Elmendorf & Suttles vs Harris vs Galloway) disagree on some mid/high patterns, taken as idiolectal or free variation (p. 32). Bianco 1998: 21 of 700+ Cowichan di-/trisyllabic roots anomalous; roots with long vowels excluded. Suttles (via Wikipedia): exceptions like xəmén 'enemy', nə́c̕aʔ 'one'.
new_statements.domain_note: Galloway's statements concern the phonological word including citation forms; high stress has a special extra-high allophone before a weakened word boundary and sentence stress/downstep can lower a word's high stress to mid in phrases (pp. 29-31; dictionary 2009 intro treats the three levels as lexical tones, high/mid/low, for Upriver only, stating Downriver and Island have 'phonemic stress plus some intonation'). Bianco 1998 covers unaffixed roots only.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted grammar (Galloway 1977) describes the Chilliwack dialect = Upriver Halkomelem (Glottolog chil1281 under upri1241), the one dialect group analysed as having pitched stress / tone (Galloway 2009 calls the three levels high/mid/low tone and says Downriver and Island Halkomelem instead have plain phonemic stress). Bianco 1998 describes Cowichan (cowi1241, Island Halkomelem isla1280); Suttles 2004 and Shaw et al. 1999 describe Musqueam (musq1240, Downriver down1241). All fall under language-level halk1245; the stress-placement facts (phonemic, default-early, full-vowel-over-schwa, morphologically shifted) appear broadly shared, but the tonal reinterpretation is Upriver-only.

new_statements.reading: Upriver (Chilliwack) Halkomelem word stress is phonemic (three pitched-stress degrees) and not positionally fixed: it may fall on any syllable from either edge, with only statistical tendencies toward the first/second syllable or the last three; stress under affixation follows stem-shape-specific rules (sec. 2.3.1). For the Island dialect, Bianco 1998 (pp. 60-61, on file) instead gives a leftmost-syllable default overridden by vowel sonority (>95% of Cowichan roots); the two statements concern different dialects, not a contradiction.

sources.citation: Hukari, Thomas E. 1978. Halkomelem Nonsegmental Morphology. 13th ICSL, pp. 157-209 (Kinkade Collection, UBCWPL).
sources.note: Cowichan: stress treated as part of nonsegmental morphology -- reduplicative/imperfective/diminutive formations involve restressing rules and reduction of unstressed vowels; stress tends to fall on tense (non-schwa) vowels; no general word-level placement rule stated (two-column scan, poor scanned).

sources.citation: Brown, Jason & James J. Thompson. 2005. Is Upriver Halkomelem a tone language? Papers for ICSNL 40, UBCWPL, pp. 49-64.
sources.quote: Following Elmendorf & Suttles, Galloway (1991, 1993) has described the Upriver dialect as something of a pitch accent language. For example, Galloway claims that: "The Upriver dialects of Halkomelem have three degrees of phonemic pitched stress or phonemic tone: /'/ high pitch-stress or high tone, /`/ mid pitch-stress or mid tone, and (unmarked) low pitch unstressed or low tone." (1993:38).
sources.note: Second-hand relay of Galloway 1993 (the grammar Zimmermann 2013 presumably draws on): Upriver Halkomelem has three phonemic degrees of pitched stress/tone; the paper itself is about whether the system is tonal (pitch phonetics), not about where stress falls.

sources.citation: Wikipedia (English), 'Halkomelem', section 'Stress and pitch' (paraphrasing Suttles 2004 Musqueam Reference Grammar, no page given).
sources.note: Second-hand for Musqueam: three stress levels; one primary stress per full word but 'its occurrence is not completely predictable'; in uninflected polysyllables primary stress usually on the first vowel (céləx, léləm̕), exceptions (xəmén); full vowel wins over schwa; rare minimal pairs (mə̀k̕ʷət vs mək̕ʷə́t); secondary stress mostly root + stressed suffix.

sources.citation: Bianco, Violet. 1998. Stress Assignment in Halkomelem-Cowichan Roots. Papers for the 33rd International Conference on Salish and Neighbouring Languages (UBCWPL), pp. 60-76.
sources.quote: In this paper I will argue that alternations in stress patterns in Cowichan are determined in part by a tendency toward overall assignment of stress to the leftmost syllable, and in part by a sonority hierarchy of vowels such that more sonorous vowels attract stress away from less sonorous vowels. I will show how the interaction of constraints concerning directionality and the relative sonority of syllable nuclei account for the placement of stress for more than 95% of Cowichan roots. [pp. 60-61]

sources.note: Intro p. x: 'The three phonemic tones are sometimes called high-stress, mid-stress, and unstressed, but actually are high tone, mid tone, and low tone... These tones can make a difference in meaning (qwá:l mosquito vs qwà:l talk)... (Downriver Halkomelem and Island Halkomelem do not have such phonemic tones so far as is known, they have instead phonemic stress plus some intonation.)' No placement rule; entries mark stress-shift as a morphological process throughout.
